AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: This study examined symptoms of anxiety and depression among college students with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

AbstractText.Label: PARTICIPANTS
AbstractText.content: Data were collected between March 2011 and March 2016 from 150 college students with ADHD and 150 college students without ADHD.

AbstractText.Label: METHOD
AbstractText.content: Participants with ADHD were compared to a sex- and ethnicity-matched control group. For the ADHD group, parent and self-report of anxiety and depression were also compared.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: College students with ADHD self-reported significantly higher anxiety and depressive symptoms than did students without ADHD. Scores on parent-report measures of anxiety and depressive symptoms were significantly higher than scores on self-report measures. Significant sex differences were found for participants with ADHD, with females showing higher depressive and anxiety symptoms than males. Parent-reported anxiety symptoms were higher for those with inattentive type ADHD compared to combined type ADHD.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: The current study highlights the importance of multi-informant assessment in ADHD evaluations for college-aged adults.
